learningObjective: Set up service endpoints and private endpoints for Azure PaaS services, including firewall rules and private DNS, and choose between them.
engineer: Service endpoints, how to set up: turn one on for a subnet and a service (Microsoft.Storage, Microsoft.Sql, Microsoft.KeyVault…). Then add a virtual network rule on the service's firewall.
Service endpoints, what changes: the service now sees the VM's private IP as the source. So old IP rules for your public IPs stop matching for those VMs.
Service endpoints, limits: they don't work from on-premises, and usually not from peered VNets. Service endpoint policies can limit traffic to specific storage accounts. They are free.

Private endpoints: a network card (NIC) with a private IP in your subnet, connected to one part of a service (for example blob, file, or sqlServer). They work from peered VNets and from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute. After adding one, you can turn public network access off. Billed per hour and per GB.

Private endpoint DNS, the usual problem: the public name (stcontoso.blob.core.windows.net) points (CNAME) to stcontoso.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. A private DNS zone, privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, linked to the VNet, answers with the private IP.
On-premises DNS: on-premises DNS must forward these names to Azure, for example through Azure DNS Private Resolver.
Approval: a private endpoint connection is approved automatically if you have rights on the resource. Otherwise the resource owner approves it by hand.
NSGs and route tables (UDRs) on private endpoints: turn on network policies on the subnet if you want them to apply.

example.title: Locking down a storage account in two steps
body: Step 1: the team turns on the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app and adds a VNet rule. As expected, the old IP rule for the NAT IP stops working for those VMs.
Step 2: the office needs access too. They add a private endpoint for blob, a linked privatelink DNS zone and a DNS Private Resolver. Then they set public network access to Disabled.

architectureDecisions: Private endpoints: when on-premises needs access, to stop data leaving to other accounts, and to turn public access off.
Service endpoints: for simple, free subnet-only access inside one region.
One place for DNS: keep the privatelink DNS zones in the hub.

misconceptions.myth: Service endpoints give the service a private IP.
misconceptions.reality: No. The service keeps its public IP. Only the source address and the path change.

misconceptions.myth: Private endpoints need no DNS changes.
misconceptions.reality: No. Clients must resolve the name to the private IP.

comparisons.service: AWS VPC gateway endpoints and interface endpoints
comparisons.difference: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are like service endpoints. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) are like private endpoints.
Lets you offer your own service, behind a Standard load balancer, to others through private endpoints.

troubleshooting.symptom: After turning on a service endpoint, VMs get 403 from storage.
troubleshooting.cause: Storage now sees the private IP, so the old IP rule doesn't match.

troubleshooting.symptom: The private endpoint exists, but the name resolves to a public IP.
troubleshooting.cause: The private DNS zone isn't linked, or the record is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Link privatelink.blob.core.windows.net to the VNet, and add a DNS zone group.

troubleshooting.symptom: Office computers can't use the private endpoint.
troubleshooting.cause: On-premises DNS doesn't know the privatelink zone.
troubleshooting.fix: Forward those names to Azure DNS Private Resolver.

configuration.limits: Private endpoints are billed per hour and per GB
One private endpoint for each part you need (blob, file, queue…)
configuration.permissions: Network Contributor on the resource group
